---
title: "PyMRM Gallery"
subtitle: "Published chemical engineering models, reproduced against their original data"
---

## What this is

A growing, open collection of the important phenomenological models of chemical
engineering — packed beds, fluidised beds, bubble columns, membrane reactors,
catalyst particles, and the unit operations next door — each one reproduced with
[`pymrm`](https://github.com/multiscale-modelling-multiphase-flows/pymrm) and
shown **against the experimental data it was originally validated on**.

Every page carries the same four things:

1. the model **as originally published**, in the original notation;
2. the **core experimental data**, as a plain CSV with full provenance;
3. the **pymrm reproduction**, overlaid on that data with a quantitative
   agreement metric;
4. **what pymrm adds** — a relaxed assumption, a finer discretisation, a limit
   the original could not reach. Or an honest statement that the page is a
   faithful reproduction and adds nothing.

Every page is a Jupyter notebook you can download and run, unmodified, in Google
Colab.

[Browse the gallery](gallery.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Three ways to use it

**Find a model and adapt it.** Filter the [gallery](gallery.qmd) by physical
domain (`sec:`) to find a model of your system, then edit the parameters. Each
page ends with a *Reuse* section listing exactly what to change.

**Find a *structure* and adapt it.** More powerful, and less obvious: filter by
`struct:` instead. A diffusion-limited enzyme pellet, a catalyst pellet, and the
solid phase of a lithium-ion battery electrode are the *same mathematical
problem*, so the same pymrm code solves all three. If nothing in your field
matches, something in someone else's probably does.

**Let a coding agent do it.** The catalog is published as machine-readable
[`models.yaml`](https://github.com/pymrm/pymrm-gallery/blob/main/models.yaml)
and the repository carries an
[`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/pymrm/pymrm-gallery/blob/main/AGENTS.md) with
instructions. Point your agent at the repository and ask it to build a model of
your system; it is designed to find the structurally nearest page and adapt it
rather than assemble something from API documentation.

## Status

Early. The [literature survey](https://github.com/pymrm/pymrm-gallery/tree/main/docs)
catalogues **266 models** across ten sections; pages are being built in priority
order, sequenced by data availability rather than by model importance.

Contributions are welcome and individually credited — see
[Contribute](contributing.qmd).
